title: The master of forgiveness
hook: O Allah, You are my Lord, You created me and I am Your servant … whoever says it with certainty in the morning (Bukhari)
tomorrow: can one line, said three times, keep you safe until morning?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lifelong reading: a portion you can keep, not a race. The book, for life. Today a new stretch begins, the short daily remembrances, and it opens with an apology.

Some apologies make it worse. Sorry you feel that way. Sorry, but. The fast sorry that's really asking the other person to drop it. Then there's the kind that lands: the one that names what the other person has done for you, and what you did, plainly, without a single 'but'. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught a line for asking God's forgiveness and called it the master of them all, sayyid al-istighfar. Its shape is the shape of the apology that lands.
screen: `SORRY, BUT.` → `THE APOLOGY THAT LANDS.` → `THE MASTER OF THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: It's in Sahih al-Bukhari, and in plain English it goes like this. O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me, and I am Your servant, and I keep Your covenant and promise as much as I can. I seek refuge in You from the harm of what I have done. I admit Your favor upon me, and I admit my sin, so forgive me, for no one forgives sins but You. Look at the order. It doesn't open with the mistake. It opens with who's who: You are my Lord, I am Your servant. Then an honest promise: as much as I can, not a perfect one. Then two admissions side by side, Your favor on me, and my sin. That pairing is the thing to tell a friend tonight: forgiveness is asked by naming the gift and the fault in one breath. And the hadith gives it weight. Whoever says it during the day with certainty and dies before evening is among the people of Paradise, and the same for the night. With certainty means meaning it, not reciting past it. Between people, the shape still teaches something. Not a script to read to anyone, but a way to stand: you've been good to me; here's what I did; I'm asking. You are my lord.
screen: `WHO'S WHO, FIRST.` · `AS MUCH AS I CAN.` · `YOUR FAVOR, AND MY SIN.` · `WITH CERTAINTY.` · then, large: `YOU ARE MY LORD.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and make two short columns on any scrap of paper. On the left, one good thing done for you this week, by a person, or, if you pray, by God. On the right, one thing you did that you'd take back. Look at the two side by side, the favor and the fault, and stay with them for the rest of the sit.
screen: `TWO COLUMNS.` · `THE FAVOR. THE FAULT.` · `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sayyid al-istighfar: the master of asking forgiveness. A line from the hadith that names the favor and the sin, side by side.
Your line: you are my lord. Then the favor, then the fault, and no 'but'. The remembrances begin.

fork.setup: a teammate misses the pass that cost the game, and in the group chat writes 'sorry, but the ref…'. what would the master of forgiveness change?
options: add more detail on why the ref really was the problem.
drop the 'but'; name what the team gave her, and what she did.
nothing; an apology in a group chat doesn't count anyway.
fork.reveal: the line names the favor and the fault side by side, and makes no excuse. that's what makes it land.

chat.meaning: Sayyid al-istighfar names the favor and the sin side by side, with no excuse. The same shape makes an apology land.

notes: The full wording of sayyid al-istighfar is given as a plain-English paraphrase of Bukhari 6306, not a published translation; confirm it is faithful (no new prayer is written).

'Whoever says it during the day with firm faith and dies before evening is of the people of Paradise; and at night likewise': Bukhari 6306. The index says 'in the morning'; the hadith says by day and by night.
Life shape: the teach's last lines apply the shape between people as 'a way to stand', not as words to say to a person. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that application.
